A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research system, renamed from FedJETs to DDOME, with matching algorithms and retained CIFAR experiments. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original CIFAR10/CIFAR100 experiments, including baseline comparisons, ablations, incremental-learning tests, and gating analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds EMNIST and Yahoo! Answers classification results.

M1.justification: The frozen common expert, softmax gating, client-level top-K selection, anchor-client mechanism, training losses, aggregation, and per-sample inference selection remain unchanged. TinyBERT supplies an expert configuration for the new text benchmark; it does not introduce a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v3 adds EMNIST ByClass handwritten-character classification and Yahoo! Answers text classification using question titles and content. These substantially extend the earlier CIFAR-only coverage. The existing Dirichlet, incremental-learning, and unseen-client scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain FedMix, FedAvg, FedProx, Average Ensembles, and Scaffold where previously reported. FedSR and FedADG remain in the domain-generalization comparison. The new benchmark tables reuse existing comparators.

E3.justification: The new text evaluation introduces pretrained TinyBERT experts, a balanced 50,000-training/10,000-test subset, question-only inputs, and batch size 16. DDOME uses SGD with exponential learning-rate decay, while text baselines use SGDM. EMNIST adds a five-label-per-client partition. Existing CIFAR protocols are largely retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds an EMNIST sensitivity observation: lower-quality common experts, such as 67% accuracy, did not support improvement by the evaluated methods. The extensive CIFAR initialization, anchor-ratio, incremental-learning, gating, and clustering analyses already appear in v2 and are retained, with several relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces experimental confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty summaries. The ensemble baseline's use of different random seeds and the existing checkpoint-based reporting practices remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New Tables 2–3 report DDOME accuracies of 64.55%/74.90% on Yahoo! Answers and 79.9%/80.5% on EMNIST under two common-expert initializations. Matched CIFAR numerical tables retain their values. The new Yahoo prose incorrectly says FedProx exceeds the common expert in one setting: Table 2 gives 60.15%/61.18% against 61%/69%.

T1.justification: v3 adds a Gaussian-input, top-1-routing linear-expert formulation and Theorem 1 asserting nonvanishing parameter error and test loss after sequential expert-then-router training. Appendix J adds assumptions, lemmas, and a proof. v2 contains optimization definitions but no corresponding theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: v2 centers on just-in-time FL personalization and leaves theoretical understanding and NLP applications to future work. v3 makes the necessity of joint gating-expert training a central contribution and claims image-and-text validation. The abstract's reported improvement changes from up to 18% to 4–24%.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit limitations concerning communication overhead relative to single-model methods, limited scalability testing, and potentially expensive gating tuning. Its meta-analysis card adds qualifications about anchor-selection knowledge and incomplete non-Gaussian theory. New interpretations address Yahoo model drift, checkpoint selection, and interference when all experts are transmitted.

D1.justification: v3 newly reports A6000/A40 hardware, approximately six-hour image training, over 100-hour text training, and 2–10 workers, alongside new benchmark preparation and initialization details. Conversely, Table 1 replaces the earlier ensemble training-round counts with dashes. The core CIFAR implementation documentation remains.

R1.justification: The paper repositions its contribution from an FL personalization system toward resolving a foundational question about joint training and MoE specialization, presenting decentralized learning as an instantiation. Bibliographic changes are limited: EMNIST, TinyBERT, and Yahoo! Answers references are added, while the neuroscience motivation and Barlow reference are removed.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and method name, adds a full-page meta-analysis card, and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, overview, and conclusion. It integrates system details into the overview, moves the main ablations into Appendix E, and adds dedicated theory and limitations sections.

P2.justification: v3 adds two benchmark tables and a styled meta-analysis card, removes the standalone common-expert diagram, and substantially changes typography and float placement. Existing ablation plots are relocated and enlarged. The retained sampling-ratio figure also corrects the CIFAR dataset assignments in its panel caption.

improvement.justification: The added benchmarks, resource disclosures, and explicit limitations improve empirical breadth and transparency. However, the newly central theoretical claim has unresolved support: Section 3 uses input covariance I_d/sqrt(d), Appendix J uses I_d/d, and its Hessian decomposition omits the corresponding 1/d factor. The new Yahoo discussion also contradicts Table 2 about FedProx. These benefits and new reliability problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
